subject: Physics
description: Understand electric current, voltage, resistance, circuits and electrical power.

concepts.title: Electric Current
concepts.description: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.
concepts.example: If 10 coulombs of charge flow through a wire in 2 seconds, the current is 10 / 2 = 5 A.
key_points: Current is the flow of electric charge.
Its SI unit is Ampere.
An ammeter measures electric current.

concepts.title: Electric Potential Difference
concepts.description: Potential difference is the work done per unit charge to move a charge between two points.
concepts.example: If 20 joules of work moves 5 coulombs of charge, the potential difference is 20 / 5 = 4 V.
key_points: Potential difference drives electric current.
Its SI unit is Volt.
A voltmeter measures potential difference.

concepts.title: Ohm's Law
concepts.description: At constant temperature, the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
concepts.example: If current is 2 A and resistance is 5 ohms, voltage = 2 × 5 = 10 V.
key_points: Voltage is directly proportional to current.
Resistance remains constant under constant physical conditions.
The V-I graph is a straight line for an ohmic conductor.

concepts.title: Resistance
concepts.description: Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of electric current.
concepts.example: A conductor has 12 V across it and carries 3 A current. Its resistance is 12 / 3 = 4 Ω.
key_points: Resistance opposes current flow.
Resistance depends on length, area, material and temperature.
Its SI unit is Ohm.

concepts.title: Resistivity
concepts.description: Resistivity is a property of a material that describes how strongly it opposes electric current.
concepts.example: For a wire of resistivity 2 Ω m, length 3 m and area 2 m², resistance = (2 × 3) / 2 = 3 Ω.
key_points: Resistivity depends on the material.
Longer wires have greater resistance.
Thicker wires generally have lower resistance.

concepts.title: Resistors in Series
concepts.description: When resistors are connected one after another, they form a series combination.
concepts.example: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω connected in series have equivalent resistance of 10 Ω.
key_points: The same current flows through every resistor.
Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances.
Equivalent resistance is greater than any individual resistance.

concepts.title: Resistors in Parallel
concepts.description: When resistors are connected across the same two points, they form a parallel combination.
concepts.example: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω connected in parallel have equivalent resistance of 2 Ω.
key_points: The voltage across each resistor is the same.
Current divides among parallel branches.
Equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

concepts.title: Electric Power
concepts.description: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or converted.
concepts.example: A device operating at 220 V and drawing 2 A consumes 440 W of power.
key_points: Power measures the rate of energy consumption.
Its SI unit is Watt.
Electrical energy is commonly measured in kilowatt-hours.

concepts.title: Heating Effect of Electric Current
concepts.description: When electric current passes through a resistance, electrical energy is converted into heat energy.
concepts.example: If 2 A current flows through a 5 Ω resistor for 10 seconds, heat produced = 2² × 5 × 10 = 200 J.
key_points: This is Joule's law of heating.
Heat increases with the square of current.
Electric heaters and fuses use the heating effect.
